extracted.intended_audience: registrants / public_company financial statement preparers, auditors, and corporate counsel (SEC filing preparers)
extracted.subtask_description: Requirements and evaluation criteria for disclosing climate-related financial statement effects (capitalized costs, expensed expenditures, charges, losses, recoveries, carbon offsets/RECs) under Regulation S-X Rule 14-02 as adopted by the SEC.

rubrics_metrics.name: One percent quantitative disclosure threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules use a one percent threshold to determine when registrants must disclose amounts (one percent of the absolute value of the relevant denominator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one percent threshold applies to aggregated denominators (stockholders' equity or deficit for balance sheet items; income or loss before income tax expense or benefit for income statement items). The Commission considered but did not adopt higher percentages or a pure dollar-only trigger. The one percent threshold is retained to provide clarity, reduce underreporting risk, and increase consistency and comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of absolute values for disclosure thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure thresholds must be calculated using the absolute values of the relevant denominator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute values avoid confusion from debit/credit sign conventions. The final rules also require using absolute values for capitalized costs and charges in the numerator (because capitalized items can offset one another). Expenditures expensed as incurred and income-statement losses do not offset and therefore absolute values are unnecessary for those numerators.

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis dollar thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules include de minimis thresholds to limit burdens on smaller companies or situations near breakeven: $100,000 for expenditures expensed as incurred and losses (income statement), and $500,000 for capitalized costs and charges (balance sheet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one percent of the absolute value of the denominator is less than the de minimis amount, disclosure is not required until aggregate expenditures or capitalized costs equal or exceed the de minimis amount. The rule rationale notes the approximate share of registrants that would have been covered by these values in 2022 (about 17% for $100,000; 24% for $500,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregated, well-defined denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure thresholds use aggregated, well-known financial statement line items (stockholders' equity or deficit; income or loss before income tax expense or benefit) defined under U.S. GAAP and IFRS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using aggregated denominators supports registrants' ability to estimate denominators during the year, facilitates internal accounting controls and ICFR, and improves comparability across registrants relative to narrower denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate application to balance sheet and income statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure threshold is applied separately to (i) capitalized costs and charges on the balance sheet and (ii) expenditures expensed as incurred and losses in the income statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying thresholds separately may in some circumstances produce only partial disclosure of an event's effects across statements, but it is more straightforward to implement and reduces burden. Registrants are not prohibited from disclosing effects on both statements even if only one threshold is triggered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution principle: 'significant contributing factor'
rubrics_metrics.description: A registrant must attribute a cost, expenditure, charge, loss, or recovery to a severe weather event or other natural condition and disclose the entire amount when the event or condition was a 'significant contributing factor' in incurring it (Rule 14-02(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission adopted 'significant contributing factor' to promote consistency and comparability across registrants while balancing burden — disclosure is required when the event was a significant factor, but not when it was only a minor factor. The principle avoids entity-specific allocation methodologies and reduces burden because there is no allocation involved. Preparers are expected to exercise judgment; many U.S. GAAP areas use the concept of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoveries must be separately disclosed (no netting for threshold determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a registrant is required to disclose costs/expenditures/charges/losses, it must separately disclose the aggregate amount of any recoveries recognized during the fiscal year related to those items (Rule 14-02(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netting recoveries (e.g., insurance proceeds) against costs to determine whether the disclosure threshold is met is not permitted, because net amounts could obscure the magnitude of the financial effects. Registrants must also identify where recoveries are presented in the income statement and balance sheet. Recoveries are contextual information to complement the costs disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and flexible definition of 'severe weather events and other natural conditions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rules use the phrase 'severe weather events' (and include examples) and clarify that the list of examples is non-exclusive and non-exhaustive; registrants have flexibility to determine what constitutes a severe weather event or other natural condition based on their particular risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrants should consider geographic location, historical experience, and financial impact, among other factors. A registrant is not required to determine whether an event was caused by climate change to trigger Rule 14-02 disclosure. The Commission favors flexibility over a prescriptive, static list because events may vary in severity by region and evolve over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon offsets and RECs disclosure when material to climate targets/goals
rubrics_metrics.description: If carbon offsets or RECs have been used as a material component of a registrant's plan to achieve disclosed climate-related targets or goals, Rule 14-02(e) requires disclosure of: (1) aggregate amount of carbon offsets and RECs expensed, (2) aggregate amount of capitalized carbon offsets and RECs recognized, and (3) aggregate amount of losses on the capitalized carbon offsets and RECs during the fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, registrants must disclose the beginning and ending balances of capitalized carbon offsets and RECs on the balance sheet for the fiscal year, where these amounts are presented on the financial statements, and the registrant's accounting policy for carbon offsets and RECs. The Commission chose this narrower transition-activity disclosure because offsets/RECs do not present the same definitional/scoping issues as broader transition activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and segregation of disclosed amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants must separately aggregate and present (1) capitalized costs and charges on the balance sheet and (2) expenditures expensed as incurred and losses in the income statement for threshold determination and disclosure (Rules 14-02(c) and (d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amounts must be segregated based on where they are recorded under GAAP upon recognition. If the applicable threshold is met, the registrant must disclose the aggregate amounts and separately identify where on the income statement and balance sheet those amounts are presented. For carbon offsets/RECs, registrants are not required to separately determine threshold per statement; specific disclosures apply if offsets/RECs are material to the registrant's plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow GAAP for classification and reliance on audit / ICFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants must follow U.S. GAAP in determining whether costs are expensed or capitalized, and these amounts will be subject to audit and related internal controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement is intended to limit 'gaming' by classifying items to avoid thresholds, because GAAP classification and audit processes constrain misclassification. Use of aggregated, well-known GAAP line items for denominators also supports internal control procedures and ICFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual information requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosure is required, registrants must provide contextual information about the disclosed amounts (e.g., composition of costs, where amounts are presented, accounting policies for offsets/RECs, and any recognized recoveries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual information complements the quantitative disclosures and helps investors understand the financial statement effects. The rules explicitly tie recoveries and accounting-policy disclosure (for offsets/RECs) into the contextual disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'Financial Impact Metrics' and alternative triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is not adopting the previously proposed 'Financial Impact Metrics' (which would have aggregated across statements) nor adopting alternatives proposed by commenters such as only a dollar threshold or requiring disclosure of all relevant expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, the final rules focus on amounts recorded in financial statements in accordance with GAAP and use the one percent thresholds with de minimis exceptions and aggregated denominators to balance usefulness, comparability, and implementation burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification on timing and event-based disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 14-02 requires event-based disclosure for expenditures recorded during the fiscal year that are attributable to severe weather events or other natural conditions; registrants are not required to determine climate causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rules focus on specific transactions recorded in the books and records during the fiscal year to simplify when disclosure is required and avoid ambiguous start/end date issues for events whose impacts continue into the future.
